Share traditional stories, knowledge, practices, and routines relating to the parts of plants and animals.

2.text: Explore and describe characteristics of materials using their sensory observations. Use appropriate vocabulary related to their investigations.
Investigate and compare the effectiveness of different materials for building stable structures.
Investigate the properties of common liquids, solids, and gases.
Investigate and identify physical and chemical changes in different states of matter.
Identify indicators of physical and chemical changes.
Investigate the properties of light using the senses.
Investigate the properties of sound using the senses.
Investigate and identify natural and artificial sources of light and sound.
Observe and describe the behaviour of light.
Identify differences in tone, pitch, and volume when producing sounds.
Analyze the advantages and risks associated with light and sound, including the negative effects of noise and light pollution.
Identify sources of water in the natural and built environments.
Examine the relationship between water and life.
Describe the stages of the water cycle, including evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection.
Investigate how seasonal changes to local water sources influence human activity.
Demonstrate understanding of the importance of water conservation and use this developing knowledge to assess their personal and household uses of water, and create a plan to use water responsibly.
Explore traditional stories, knowledge, practices, and routines relating to water.
Describe and classify a wide range of animals according to various characteristics and behaviours.
Describe and classify a wide range of plants according to various physical characteristics and traits.
Compare the life cycles of animals and plants that have similar and different life cycles.
Investigate the physical characteristics and behaviours of animals as they grow and develop.
Investigate the physical changes in plants as they grow and develop.
Share traditional stories, knowledge, practices, and routines relating to life cycles.

3.text: Design experiments to demonstrate how matter has mass and takes up space.
Apply the understanding of chemical and physical changes to demonstrate the conversion of mass from one form to another.
Demonstrate through experiments that air has mass and takes up space like other states of matter.
Demonstrate through experiments that liquids have mass and take up space like other states of matter.
Demonstrate through experiments that solids have mass and take up space like other states of matter.
Show how atoms are arranged and spaced in different states of matter, such as solids, liquids, and gases.
Investigate the volume, shape, and mass of different states of matter through experiments.
Explain how atoms move and interact at different levels of thermal energy, illustrating the changes in their movement as temperature varies.
Design experiments to demonstrate the transfer of thermal energy through conduction, convection, and radiation.
Investigate traditional ways of manipulating thermal energy for survival.
Investigate and experiment how insulators and conductors are used to allow or stop the transfer of energy.
Design experiments or models to demonstrate the transfer of kinetic energy.
Investigate how light energy moves and changes directions.
Investigate how sound energy moves and changes directions.
Identify components and common uses of the Earth’s surface.
Examine the physical properties of rocks.
Explore and understand the process of rock formation and rock cycle.
Examine types of landforms.
Explain how climate affects the Earth’s surface, including its impact on permafrost.
Investigate traditional stories, knowledge, and uses of rocks.
Identify local habitats and biodiversity and compare it to other habitats around the world.
Explore and compare how animals and plants from different habitats use the land to meet their needs.
Consider how changes to a habitat can affect different plants and animals.
Investigate the local migration patterns of Arctic animals, and explore ideas as to why these migration patterns have changed in recent years.
Share traditional stories, knowledge, practices, and routines relating to habitats.

4.text: Compare the properties of solids, liquids, and gases.
Experiment with phase changes between solids, liquids, and gases such as evaporation and condensation, melting and freezing, evaporation and sublimation, etc.
Explore and understand the concept of density in regards to different states of matter.
Explain the relationship between density and heat.
Examine the impacts of changing states of matter on the land and its impacts on daily life in the North.
Identify and classify different forms of energy and their uses in daily life.
Understand the law of conservation of energy and its applications in daily life.
Demonstrate the law of the conservation of energy through energy transformations and apply knowledge of energy transformations to solve problems.
Experiment with devices that transform one form of energy into another.
Investigate common energy transformations.
Demonstrate safety practices and protocols for working with different forms of energy.
Investigate practices and opportunities for energy conservation.
Investigate local and territorial uses of Earth’s natural resources.
Compare and contrast renewable and non-renewable resources.
Examine the properties of rocks and minerals, and their uses.
Demonstrate the rock cycle.
Investigate the impacts of mining on the land.
Consider how our local environment affects how we live.
Share traditional stories, knowledge, practices, and routines relating to resource conservation.
Investigate the roles of a variety of plants and animals in the local ecosystem as producers, consumers, and decomposers.
Construct food chains and webs to demonstrate the transfer of energy and show understanding of how all organisms are interconnected.
Assess interdependent relationships in an environment and explore how changes to an ecosystem can affect different plants and animals.
Share traditional stories, knowledge, practices, and routines relating to interconnectedness on the land.

5.text: Identify the parts of a solution.
Share examples of everyday solutions.
Investigate factors that affect the solubility of substances in water.
Compare the viscosity of various liquids.
Apply techniques for the separation of solutions.
Explain the effects of soluble and insoluble substances on the land.
Distinguish between human-made machines and those found in nature.
Experiment with simple machines to see how they function and identify levers, wedges, inclined planes, pulleys, screws, and wheels and axles in daily life.
Design experiments to discern that using a machine lessens the amount of force required to complete a task.
Investigate traditional tools and modern tools and identify which types of simple machines they are and what type of tasks they can achieve.
Demonstrate ways to increase and decrease power.
Design or improve machines to perform specific tasks.
Begin to develop a basic understanding of units of measurement using SI and Imperial units.
Investigate how the land changes over time.
Investigate the effects of weathering and erosion on the environment.
Investigate the tectonic process.
Assess the relationship between human activity and changes to the land.
Assess how climate change affects the environment.
Investigate how Inuit ways of knowing inform protection for the land in Nunavut, the country, and the world.
Share traditional stories, knowledge, practices, and routines relating to changes to the land.
Describe the basic structures and functions of various parts of the human body.
Compare and contrasts the internal organs and body structures of mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, and amphibians.
Compare and contrast the anatomy of different plants such as trees, shrubs, bushes, ferns, herbs, perennials, deciduous, and evergreen.
Investigate how plants, animals, and humans adapt to survive in their environment.
Share traditional stories, knowledge, practices, and routines about survival adaptations.

6.text: Recognize the difference between a mixture and a solution and compare their properties.
Explore and investigate the observable properties of homogeneous mixtures.
Explore and investigate the observable properties of heterogeneous mixtures.
Analyze the observable properties of familiar homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures.
Recognize through investigation the difference between a colloid and a suspension and design experiments with colloids and suspensions to examine their properties.
Express the potentially dangerous or damaging effects of mixing materials of different properties.
Begin to investigate common techniques used to separate the components of a variety of mixtures.
Create commonly used mixtures.
Understand and describe the difference between balanced and unbalanced forces and design experiments to showcase them in action.
Explain Newton’s three laws of motion and their application in daily life.
Investigate factors that influence the force of gravity.
Understand and explore Bernoulli’s Principle of Flight and its applications in daily life.
Investigate the forces of flight applying the basic understanding of Bernoulli’s Principle.
Apply the knowledge of drag, lift, thrust, and air pressure when designing flying devices.
Demonstrate an understanding of how water contributes to Earth’s survival.
Identify, describe, and compare the different planets within our solar system.
Design models to explore the difference between rotation and revolutions.
Design a model to demonstrate Earth’s axis, rotation, and revolution around the Sun.
Investigate how Earth’s location in our solar system, galaxy, and universe makes it habitable for living things.
Compare extreme environments on Earth to outer space.
Research local and global contributions to and impacts on space exploration and technologies.
Share traditional stories, knowledge, practices, and routines related to our solar system.
Describe how parts of the human body work together as systems.
Compare the functions of different organs in the human body to those of other species and identify the differences.
Investigate how our body systems interact and work together to create a unique ecosystem.
Share traditional stories, knowledge, practices, and routines about body systems.

k.text: Activate prior knowledge by asking questions about kinship and identity.
Identify specific characteristics that make up their own unique identity (for example, personality traits, interests, hobbies, skills, and talents).
Demonstrate their own identity through verbal expression, behaviour (actions) and visual representations (images, pictures, drawings, etc.).

Demonstrate an understanding of how an awareness of others’ identities can help build healthy relationships (through celebrating differences, listening to understand others’ ideas and opinions, acknowledging others’ identities, etc.)
Demonstrate an understanding of needs versus wants and begin to ask questions about their own needs at home and at school.
Demonstrate an understanding of responsibilities and begin to identify their responsibilities at home and at school.
Identify who helps meet their needs at home and at school.
Identify ways to help their families and their classroom community.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry to contribute to building their Kindergarten community.
Explore family stories by asking questions (for example, ask questions using the 5 Ws).
Listen to and share personal stories of significance with peers.
Demonstrate an awareness of how stories help us understand ourselves and our families.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry related to stories that are significant to them and their peers.
Explore their understanding of how the land provides for us.
Demonstrate an understanding of needs and identify the things we need to live.
Demonstrate an awareness of maps as representations of real places. Represent places on the land that are important to them through images, words, maps, etc.
Make and share simple observations about the land, including weather, sky, animals, plants, water, and ice.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry to brainstorm, discuss, and plan ways to show the connection between the land and their needs.

1.text: Activate prior knowledge about different kinds of communities through discussions and questioning.
Demonstrate an understanding of what community means and identify characteristics of a healthy community.
Explore various communities in Nunavut and examine different perspectives among individuals and groups about issues affecting their local community as well as other communities in Nunavut.
Demonstrate respect and sensitivity for diversity through words, images, and actions.
Demonstrate an understanding of rights, roles, and responsibilities by exploring these concepts in the local community, through inquiry.
Demonstrate an understanding of leadership and give examples of leadership in their communities (Elders, mayor, community volunteers, etc.)
Examine how rights, roles, and responsibilities change over time and in different situations.
Demonstrate respect and sensitivity for the rights of others.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry by exploring and comparing various communities within Nunavut.
Using the 5 Ws, explore traditional stories of local and other communities.
Identify significant events and figures in the community’s past and present and demonstrate how events from the past have influenced the community today.

Explore the local community’s history by gathering information using a variety of sources, including Elders, knowledge keepers, and local visitor centers. Describe some of the ways that the local community has changed or stayed the same over time.
Sequence events from the community’s past.
Demonstrate how stories from the community’s past have influenced the community today.
Recount a significant story from their local community or another Nunavut community using information or evidence from multiple sources including Elders and community knowledge keepers.
Explore their understanding of the impact of human actions on the land.
Describe how people use the natural and human-made features in and around the community to meet their needs.
Describe how the land shapes life in the community.
Identify different local Inuktut place names and explain how they describe the land. Describe local Inuit landmarks and significant places.
Construct and use maps that represent the local community and the surrounding land. Identify significant places on the map, including community landmarks.
Make and share observations about the land, including weather, sky, animals, plants, water, and ice. Give examples of how daily life is influenced by the environment/land.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry related to how the relationship of their community to the land can be strengthened.

2.text: Activate prior knowledge about communities in Canada through discussions and questioning.
Explore the physical features of several communities in Canada. Identify and compare these features.
Identify communities on a map of Canada and explore the diversity among the land and people.
Demonstrate an awareness of factors that influence diversity among and between Canadian communities.
Explore their rights as Canadians through inquiry.
Identify some of the rights and responsibilities shared by Canadians.
Explore the various types of leadership practised in Canadian communities and compare these leadership practises to their local communities or other known communities.
Describe how Canadians’ rights and responsibilities may have changed over time and may not always be fulfilled.
Investigate examples of when rights and responsibilities have been neglected in Canada and describe some of the consequences.
Collaborate and work together with peers in an Authentic Inquiry to explore and engage with a Canadian community outside of Nunavut.
Activate prior knowledge about the purposes of stories.
Identify past events in other places (including events from other Nunavut communities) that significantly shaped their local community.

Explore another Nunavut community’s history by gathering information using a variety of sources, including Elders, knowledge keepers, and visitor centers. Describe some of the ways that the community has changed and stayed the same over time.
Explore stories from the past from different regions in Nunavut or communities outside of Nunavut. Demonstrate awareness of how these stories from the past can help shape the community today.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry about a significant story of a community.
Explore their current understanding of the movement of air, water, and animals.

Explore how the water, air, and some animals circulate over great distances. Demonstrate understanding of maps through the use of cardinal directions and through distinguishing between land and water masses on maps.
Identify ways that the land here can be affected by human activity in other places. Demonstrate care and concern for the land in their actions (for example, the 3 Rs, community clean-up, etc.).
Make and share observations about unusual changes in the land, including weather, sky, animals, plants, water, and ice.
Demonstrate awareness of how everyone is responsible for Avatimik Kamattiarniq (environmental stewardship).
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry related to how people’s relationship to land is changing, here and elsewhere, and the possible consequences.

3.text: Activate prior knowledge by exploring questions about Indigenous Peoples in Canada and the world.
Demonstrate an awareness of their own Inuit heritage and culture, and compare their way of life to Indigenous Peoples elsewhere.
Learn about Indigenous Peoples in other parts of Canada and the world, and use maps to identify and represent Indigenous Peoples in other parts of Canada and the world.
Activate prior knowledge about rights and responsibilities and inquire about Indigenous Peoples in Canada and in other parts of the world.
Identify common rights and responsibilities of Indigenous Peoples in Canada and in other parts of the world.
Investigate challenges faced by Indigenous Peoples in Canada and in other parts of the world with respect to rights and around responsibilities.
Explore the role of leadership in maintaining rights and responsibilities and identify formal and informal types of leadership.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry to explore shared experiences of diverse Indigenous Peoples in Canada and the world.
Through discussions and questions, explore how we learn about the past.
Demonstrate an awareness of how accounts and evidence of the past may vary according to different perspectives.
Summarize an oral narrative and explain its significance. Demonstrate awareness that oral tradition/narrative are a source of historical information.
Demonstrate an awareness of the significance of Inuit oral narrative in understanding the past.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry to develop and share an oral narrative about a significant event.
Explore their current understanding of Inuit beliefs about respecting the land through questioning.
Identify various Inuit practises that demonstrate respect for the land.
Describe some of the potential consequences of being disrespectful to the land.
Explore the relationship Indigenous People in other parts of Canada have with the land.

Construct and use maps that show places of cultural significance for Inuit or Indigenous Peoples in another place. Identify the continents and oceans on a map or globe and identify regions, countries, or places on a map that are of cultural significance for Inuit or other Indigenous Peoples.
Make and share observations about unusual changes to the land, including weather, sky, animals, plants, water, and ice, and how these affect the local community.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry related to Inuit and other Indigenous Peoples’ knowledge about living well with the land.

4.text: Activate prior knowledge about the movement of people within and to the North.
Demonstrate an understanding of migration and explore reasons people move to new places.
Explore Inuit way of life prior to the arrival of non-Inuit. Demonstrate an understanding of the transition that has occurred in the North since the arrival of non-Inuit.
Activate prior knowledge about Nunavut’s creation through inquiry.
Explore the creation of Nunavut as a territory and identify reasons Inuit leaders fought to create Nunavut.
Examine the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement and identify areas related to protecting land, culture, and language. Explore the significance of this connection.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry related to ways that the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement addresses the needs of Inuit in Nunavut.
Explore their current understanding of contact between Inuit and non-Inuit by asking questions.
Explore life in the North before the arrival of nonInuit by examining different types of evidence.
Explore the different stages of contact with nonInuit and compare how Inuit life changed during the different stages.
Explore and describe significant events influencing Inuit in Nunavut.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry examining to what extent has Inuit resilience has played a role in responding to colonization.
Explore their current understanding about land ownership by asking questions.
Explore how different beliefs about the land can lead to different types of land use.
Explore the positive and negative influences of different types of industry in Northern Canada.
Explore the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement and identify ways it may help to protect the land.
Make, record, and share observations about human impacts on the land, including weather, sky, animals, plants, water, and ice.
Identify the provinces, territories, and capital cities in Canada on a map, and use maps to show places in Northern Canada that require environmental protection.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry assessing the choices involved in a current or historic land-use project in Northern Canada.

5.text: Ask questions about immigration to and movement of people within Canada.
Explore some of the reasons people have immigrated to Canada and the impacts of this immigration.
Demonstrate an understanding of the ways in which immigration and multiculturalism have influenced Canadian identity.
Activate prior knowledge by exploring and asking questions about different regions in Canada.
Demonstrate an awareness of the resources and the areas of need for the different regions in Canada.
Use maps to demonstrate the diverse resources of Canada’s regions.
Demonstrate an awareness that there are different levels of government in Canada with different responsibilities (for example, municipal, territorial, federal, Inuit, etc.)
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry related to the economic inequality among Canada’s regions and possible solutions.
Explore current understanding of diverse stories from Canada’s past.
Examine significant stories and diverse perspectives about peoples in Canada and Canada’s past using different types of evidence.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry related to a significant event in the development of Canada that affected different people in different ways.
Explore their current understanding of landuse decisions in Canada by asking questions.
Make connections between natural resources, economic activities, ways of life, identity, and land-use decisions.
Demonstrate awareness of the impact of economic activities on the land in Canada using evidence and various sources.
Identify key physical features of Northern Canada on a map (such as landforms, bodies of water, etc.) and use maps to compare traditional and contemporary land use.
Identify the provinces, territories, and capital cities in Canada on a map, and use maps to show places in Northern Canada that require environmental protection.
Demonstrate ways that being connected to the land can help people make wise land-use decisions.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry related to how the relationship of their own community or another Canadian community to the land is changing.

6.text: Activate prior knowledge about countries helping others. Explore the term foreign aid.
Identify specific ways that Canadians help people in other countries.
Investigate how organizations around the world work together to address global issues.
Demonstrate an understanding of different types of international cooperation.
Use maps to demonstrate and interpret the need for international cooperation and aid around the world.
Activate prior knowledge about governments and human rights through inquiry.
Demonstrate understanding of the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights by examining the core principles of human rights.
Compare how different types of national and international governments address and protect human rights.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry related to how the world can work together to reduce global disparity.
Explore their understanding of where we get information about current events through questioning.
Demonstrate awareness of the significance of media in governance.
Demonstrate an understanding of bias and identify bias in different types of media.
Explore how and why bias may influence stories or the reporting of events.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry related to the presence and impact of bias in the media and test the reliability of a variety of media sources.
Explore their understanding of land-use conflicts with discussion and questioning.
Describe how different perspectives on land use can create conflict.
Demonstrate awareness of the impact of human activity on the environment.
Identify on a map of Canada, places, and regions of historical significance, including existing or potential land-use conflicts.
Explore and share potential challenges to land changes including climate, animals, water, and ice.
Collaborate and work together with peers in Authentic Inquiry to examine a past or present conflict over land use and propose a viable resolution.
